title: Lecture 6 – Adrenal glands
html:
Source: CursVI adrenals-MGE 2022 Oct.pptx – 68 slides

THE ADRENAL GLANDS #1

Topics: #2

  • Chronic adrenocortical insufficiency
  • Acute adrenocortical insufficiency
  • Congenital adrenal hyperplasia:21-hydroxylase deficiency
  • Cushing syndrome
  • Primary aldosteronism
  • Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma

Anatomy #3

  • -paired organs adjacent to the kidneys, containing:
  • a cortex
  • a medulla→epinephrine (E), norepinephrine (NE), small amounts of dopamine

Slide 4 #4

  • The adrenal cortex – 3 functional and morphological different zones ( with enzymatic differences and with differing regulation and secretory products, as well)
  • glomerulosa (lacks 17-hydroxylase activity) secreting mineralocorticoids-Aldosterone, DOC(deoxycorticosterone)
  • fasciculata secreting glucocorticoids(cortisol) and androgens
  • +
  • -reticularis secreting adrenal androgens (dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), DHEA sulfate and androstendione ) and cortisol
  • (do not express the gene CYP11B2 (encoding P450aldo) and therefore cannot convert 11-DOC to aldosterone )
  • the inner two zones appear to function as a unit

Slide 5 #5

  • ACTH= a polypeptide (cleaved from prohormone POMC), secreted in a pulsatile fashion from the anterior pituitary with diurnal variability (peak: 0200-0400; trough: 1800-2400)
  • • secretion regulated by corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) and arginine vasopressin (AVP)
  • • stimulates growth of adrenal cortex and release of glucocorticoids, androgens and, to a limited extent, mineralocorticoids

Glucocorticoid and androgen #6

  • productions ( the zonae fasciculata
  • and reticularis) are under the control of
  • ACTH, which regulates both steroid synthesis and also adrenal growth;
  • excess or deficiency of this hormone alters their structure and function
  • → ↑ ACTH: hyperplasia and hypertrophy of these zones occur+ ↑production of cortisol and androgens
  • → ↓ ACTH:both zones atrophy +↓production of cortisol and androgens
  • !!! Only cortisol is responsible of the negative FB on the CRH and ACTH secretion
  • Glucocorticoids and adrenal androgens
  • Regulation of Secretion

The synthesis of aldosterone by the zona glomerulosa is primarily regulated by- #7

  • -the renin-angiotensin system (RAS)
  • - potassium
  • - (lesser extent ACTH )
  • → in ACTH deficiency- aldosterone secretion remains normal except in a few cases.
  • The adrenal androgens,
  • DHEA,
  • DHEA-sulfate,
  • androstendione
  • have minimal intrinsic androgenic activity, and they contribute to androgenity by their peripheral conversion to the more potent androgens testosterone(T) and DHT.

ADRENOCORTICAL INSUFFICIENCY PRIMARY ADRENOCORTICAL INSUFFICIENCY (ADDISON DISEASE) #8

  • Adrenocortical insufficiency (ACI) is a rare disease having a prevalence of 10–15 per 100 000 population, characterized by deficient adrenal production of glucocorticoids and/or mineralocorticoids
  • CLASSIFICATIONS
  • According to the location of lesion
  • Primary ACI← either the consequence of destruction or dysfunction of the cortex
  • Central ACI ←secondary to deficient pituitary ACTH secretion
  • ! Glucocorticoid therapy (to treat a large variety of illnesses) is the most common cause of secondary adrenocortical insufficiency
  • Chronic use of corticosteroids inhibits the function of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis by negative feedback, which may cause adrenal insufficiency after the cessation of corticosteroid treatment
  • According to evolution
  • Chronic ACI
  • Acute ACI

Slide 9 #9

  • Table 1. ETIOLOGY (excluding congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH)) and Pathology
  • PRIMARY ADRENOCORTICAL INSUFFICIENCY (ADDISON DISEASE)
Autoimmune ( the most common cause in developed countries- 70%) Sporadic Type 1 or 2 autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes ( APS)
Infiltrations: amyloidosis, hemochromatosis, sarcoidosis
Infections: Tuberculosis (prior to 1920, was the major cause ), funguses, CMV, HIV
Adrenal haemorrhage/infarction: Anticoagulant therapy Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome (meningococcal septicaemia) The primary antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (lupus anticoagulant)
Congenital adrenal hypoplasia (mutations/deletion of the NR0B1(DAX-1) or the NR5A1 (SF-1) genes.)
Adrenoleukodystrophy (X-linked, is an important cause of ACI in men; abnormal accumulation of very long chain fatty acids (VLCFAs) in the brain, adrenal cortex, testes, and liver )
Metastatic adrenal disease (common sites of metastasis for lung, gastrointestinal, breast, and renal neoplasia)
Iatrogenic Bilateral adrenalectomy Drugs: ketoconazole, abiraterone, etomidate, aminoglutethimide (inhibit cortisol bioshynthesis), mitotane(adrenolytic),

Slide 10 #10

  • Autoimmune Addison’s disease is frequently accompanied by other immune disorders; there are 2 different syndromes, known as autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes ( APS) in which ACI may occur
  • APS, type I: hypoparathyroidism, chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, ACI, gonadal failure, hypothyroidism, DM type 1, DI+ nonendocrine diseases: alopecia, pernicious anemia, chronic active hepatitis
  • APS type II: ACI, autoimmune thyroid disease, gonadal failure, DM type1, DI+ celiac sprue, vitiligo, pernicious anemia, myasthenia gravis (also known as Schmidt’s syndrome)

CLINICAL FEATURES IN PRIMARY ACI (ADDISON’S DISEASE) #11

  • 1.Hyperpigmentation
  • (=the classic physical finding) of the skin and mucous membranes – generalized;
  • ↑ in sun-exposed areas and over pressure areas such as the knuckles, elbows, knees;
  • ↑pigmentation of the palmar creases, nail beds, nipples, areolae and perivaginal and perianal mucosa;
  • The classic hyperpigmentation of the buccal mucosa and gums comes after the generalized hyperpigmentation of the skin;
  • Scars that have formed after the onset of ACTH excess become hyperpigmented, whereas older ones do not!

CLINICAL FEATURES IN PRIMARY ACI (ADDISON’S DISEASE) #12

  • 2. General weakness and fatigue, malaise
  • anorexia, weight loss (!!! 15 kg)
  • 3. CV symptoms :hypotension (≈90% of patients, accompanied by orthostatic symptoms: dizziness and occasionally syncope)
  • orthostasis or orthostatic hypotension is  Positive Schellong test (a reduction in systolic BP of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic BP of at least 10 mmHg within 3 min of standing)
  • 4.Gastrontestinal disturbances: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea or constipation, abdominal pain, salt craving
  • Salt craving occurs in about 20% of patients.
  • Arthralgia; myalgia
  • Hypoglycemia (sweats, tremor, headache)
  • irritability, emotional instability, depression
  • loss of axillary and pubic hair-in women (← ↓ secretion of adrenal androgens)
  • Vitiligo occurs in 4% to 17% of patients with autoimmune Addison disease

DIAGNOSIS OF ACI- INVESTIGATIONS #13

  • The diagnosis of ACI requires three steps.
  • I.First, the function of the adrenal cortex should be assessed -Establish the diagnosis of ACI
  • The diagnostic test for primary ACI should be paired measurement of serum cortisol and plasma ACTH.
  • Single cortisol measurements are of little value, although a random cortisol below 100 nmol/L during the day is highly suggestive, (and undetectable serum cortisol is usually diagnostic of ACI) and a random cortisol higher than 550 nmol/L makes the diagnosis unlikely.
  • ↓/undetectable cortisol +↑↑ ACTH= overt primary ACI
  • Normal values cortisol: 8 a.m. -70-220 ng/ml (5-25 microgr/dl); 171-550nmol/l
  • 6-8 pm 2.5-13.0 microgr/dl (71.1-286 nmol/L)
  • 12 am <7 microgr/dl
  • -in many patients with partial ACI, basal levels of cortisol in plasma may be normal or low-normal; simultaneous 9 a.m. ACTH and cortisol measurement in these patients will show an ↑ ACTH for the level of cortisol (→ partial primary ACI).
  • This (↑ACTH) is a very sensitive means of detecting Addison’s disease.
  • If both the serum cortisol and plasma ACTH concentrations are inappropriately ↓, the patient has secondary (ie, pituitary disease) or tertiary (hypothalamic disease) adrenal insufficiency
  • Unfortunately, plasma ACTH results are usually not available immediately
  • 

ACI #14

  •  The short (rapid) ACTH (Synacthen®)250 mcg (im or iv) stimulation test
  • (synthetic human 1-24-ACTH called tetracosactin or cosyntropin is used)
  • measures the acute adrenal response to ACTH and is used to diagnose both primary and secondary adrenal insufficiency.
  • → a synacthen stimulated (0.25 mg im or iv) peak serum cortisol <500 nmol/ L is diagnostic of ACI
  • Normal responses (peak cortisol, 30-60 minutes later, >550nmol/l (20µg/dl);
  • Note that an absent or impaired cortisol response confirms the presence of hypoadrenalism but does not differentiate Addison’s disease from ACTH deficiency or iatrogenic suppression by steroid medication.
  • Long Synacthen® test (depot Synacthen® 1mg IM)

II. Diagnosis of primary and secondary forms of ACI #15

  • Plasma ACTH 8-9 a.m.
  • Plasma ACTH levels are most useful in differentiating pituitary causes (secondary forms) from adrenal causes of adrenal insufficiency as follows:
  • ACTH plasmatic  – primary ACI
  • ACTH plasmatic  / “low-normal”– central
  • Additional laboratory investigations
  • • Plasma renin activity is high due to low serum aldosterone.
  • Hyponatremia and hyperkalemia are classic manifestations of glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency and should suggest the diagnosis – K ­↑ (acute adrenal crisis)
  • • FBC - normocytic, normochromic anemia (← altered androgen metabolism) neutropenia, eosinophilia and a relative lymphocitosis
  • • ↑concentration of blood urea nitrogen and serum creatinine (←volume depletion and dehydration)
  • • mild acidosis, mild hypercalcemia
  • • Serum glucose ↓< 70mg/dl
  • • ECG: low voltage, a vertical QRS axis, and nonspecific ST-T wave abnormalities secondary to abnormal electrolytes

III. Once PAI is confirmed, it is mandatory to establish the aetiology #16

  • TESTS FOR ETIOLOGY
  • Adrenal autoantibodies
  • (detect antibodies to adrenal cortex, specific antibodies to 21-hydroxylase, cholesterol side chain cleavage enzyme, and 17-hydroxylase)(indirect information ← testing for thyroid autoantibodies)
  • Adrenal antibodies are present in approximately 90% of cases of autoimmune adrenalitis.
  • Imaging:
  •  Adrenal enlargement, with or without calcification, may be seen on CT of the abdomen, suggesting tuberculosis, infiltrative, or metastatic disease.
  •  The adrenals are small and atrophic in chronic autoimmune adrenalitis.
  • • Percutaneous CT-guided adrenal biopsy is occasionally required (→metastatic lesions suspected).
  • • Specific tests—e.g. serological or microbiological investigations directed at particular infections (eg, tuberculosis)/ very long chain fatty acids (adrenoleukodystrophy)
  • → CENTRAL FORM
  • CT/MRI of the hypothalamus –pituitary can identify the lesion

TREATMENT OF CHRONIC ACI #17

  • Objectives:
  • Long-term: to produce-assure levels of glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids equivalent to those achieved in an individual with normal HPA function under similar circumstances.
  • !!!Patient education on how to increase steroid doses during concurrent illnesses or injury is important
  • replacement treatment (life-long gluco- and mineralocorticoid therapy)
  • Chronic MAINTENANCE THERAPY
  • GLUCOCORTICOIDS
  • Hydrocortisone or cortisone acetate (CA) is the treatment of choice for replacement therapy:15-25 mg/day, administered twice to thrice daily, e.g. 10mg HC immediately on waking, 5mg HC at midday, and 5mg HC at 4–5 p.m, or 15mgHC on waking and 5mg HC at midday
  • PREDNISONE 5-7,5 mg/day
  • A modified release hydrocortisone formulation (Plenadren) allowing once daily dosing, has recently been introduced in Europe
  • MINERALOCORTICOIDS
  • 9--fluorocortisol (fludrocortisone) (ASTONIN H) 0.1 mg/tb ½-2 tb/day- a synthetic mineralocorticoid used to replace mineralocorticoid deficiency;
  • 10% can be managed with cortisol and dietary sodium intake alone !;
  • rarely required in central adrenocortical insufficiency
  •  ANDROGENS
  • DHEA 50mg/day→ an improvement in well-being and sexual function in F
  • LIFESTYLE ADVICE – ↑ in proteins, vitamins, adequate dietary sodium intake (!!!not restriction)

Monitoring of therapy #18

  • Adequacy of glucocorticoid dose:
  • Clinical
  • • Adequate treatment results in the disappearance of weakness, malaise, and fatigue, anorexia and other gastrointestinal symptoms; the hyperpigmentation invariably improves
  • • Inadequate cortisol administration leads to persistence of these symptoms of adrenal insufficiency, and excessive pigmentation remains/ conversely, overtreatment →signs of Cushing syndrome e.g ↑ weight.
  • •
  • Biochemical
  • • Cortisol day curves + ACTH, or plasma cortisol to assess adequacy have been proposed but not yet widely adopted
  • Adequacy of fludrocortisone replacement is assessed by:
  • • restoration of serum electrolytes to normal
  • • no evidence of hypertension or postural hypotension (it should not fall >10 mmHg systolic after 2 minutes’ standing)
  • • suppression of plasma renin activity to high normal.
  • Hypertension and oedema suggest excessive mineralocorticoid replacement whereas postural hypotension and salt craving suggest insufficient treatment.

TREATMENT OF THE CHRONIC ADRENOCORTICAL INSUFFICIENCY #19

  • GENERAL MEASURES –PREVENTION OF ADRENAL CRISIS
  • The essential elements are patient education and increased glucocorticoid dosages during illness!
  • Patients must be taught never to miss a dose.
  • All patients requiring replacement steroids should:
  • • know how to increase steroid replacement by doubling the dose for intercurrent illness
  • • carry a ‘steroid card’
  • • wear a MedicAlert bracelet (or similar), which gives details of their condition so that emergency replacement therapy can be given if found unconscious
  • • keep an (up-to- date) ampoule of hydrocortisone at home in case oral therapy is impossible, for administration by self, family, ambulance or doctor.
  • Cortisol requirements increase during severe illness or surgery.
  • during period of minor stress→ the daily dose of hydrocortisone should be doubled (or 3X)
  • the dose needs to be ↑ to as much as 200-300 mg/day (iv) during periods of major stress, such as a surgical procedure;
  • ETIOLOGIC TREATEMENT
  • when it is possible (eg tuberculosis)

DEFINITION #20

  • Acute adrenal crisis represents a state of acute adrenocortical insufficiency
  • in patients with Addison disease who are exposed to the stress of infection, trauma, surgery, or dehydration due to salt deprivation, vomiting, or diarrhea (without an increase of glucocorticoid dosages during illness)
  • bilateral acute adrenal hemorrhage and CAH (represent another two possible causes)
  • Clinical picture:
  • hypotension and shock, volume depletion, dehydration,
  • hyperpyrexia (← infection or hypoadrenalism per se),
  • weakness,
  • apathy,
  • depressed mentation,
  • abdominal pain (that mimic an acute abdominal emergency) (abdominal distention, rigidity and rebound tenderness are less frequent),
  • nausea, vomiting, anorexia,
  • muscle cramps,
  • hypoglycemia.
  • Shock and coma may rapidly lead to death in untreated patients
  • ACUTE ACI(ADDISON CRISIS)

ACUTE ADRENAL CRISIS #21

  • LABORATORY FINDINGS:
  • ↓↓ CORTIZOL +
  • Additional findings that suggest the diagnosis are hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, lymphocytosis, eosinophilia, and hypoglycemia, ↑urea­, creatinine­, hematocrit­, metabolic acidosis
  • Management
  • Emergency! take blood for glycemia, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, cortisol before initiating treatment with glucocorticoids; Do not wait for lab results if the clinical features are strongly suggestive
  •  iv 0.9% saline and 5% glucose are administered to correct volume depletion, hypotension and hypoglycemia
  •  Hydrocortisone should be administered in a dosage of 100 mg intravenously followed by 50 to 75 mg every 6 hours thereafter; when the patient is stable, reduce the dosage to 50 mg every 6 h;
  • (mineralocorticoid is not necessary during the acute replacement period since enough NaCl and glucocorticoid are being administered to treat the mineralocorticoid deficiency);
  • -taper to maintenance therapy by day 4 or 5 and add mineralocorticoid.
  •  Identify and treat precipitating factor (eg, infection)
  • as required

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) #22

  • Definition
  • CAH is a group of inherited disorders characterized by a deficiency of one of the enzymes necessary for cortisol biosynthesis.
  • In many cases, CAH results in lack of cortisol and overproduction of androgen.
  • • >90% of cases are due to 21α-hydroxylase deficiency.
  • P450c21 Hydroxylase Deficiency
  • 21α-hydroxylase deficiency results from gene mutations, partial gene deletions, or gene conversions.

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia #23

  • 21α-hydroxylase deficiency results in aldosterone and cortisol deficiency.
  • Loss of –ve feedback from cortisol results in ACTH hypersecretion, and this causes adrenocortical hyperplasia and accumulation of steroid precursors ‘above’ the enzyme deficiency, including progesterone and 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17OHP).
  • These are then shunted into androgen synthesis pathways, resulting in testosterone, androstenedione, and DHT excess.

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia: 21-hydroxylase deficiency (>90%) #24

  • Clinical presentation is a consequence of the degree of enzymatic deficiency : from presentation in neonatal period with salt wasting and virilization to non-classic CAH in adulthood and depends on severity of mutation
  • Classic CAH
  • 1. Salt wasting, ambiguous genitalia in female (clitoromegaly and labial fusion at birth)
  • ← severe reduction (98%) in P450c21-hydroxylase activity→ to impaired secretion of both cortisol and aldosterone; + excess adrenal androgen synthesis
  • Because ♂ have normal genitalia at birth, they may present acutely ill in the neonatal period with vomiting, dehydration, collapse, hyponatraemia, and hyperkalaemia.
  • If untreated or poorly treated, both sexes may develop pubic hair, acne, rapid height velocity, advanced bone maturation, and precocious puberty which may result in very short final height
  • 2. Simple virilizing disease
  • ← impaired cortisol synthesis, ↑ACTH levels, and ↑adrenal androgen secretion;← some gene mutation that retain enough P450c21-hydroxylase activity to produce sufficient aldosterone to prevent hypoNa/hyperK
  • Affected ♀ have a less severe degree of masculinization of their external genitalia
  • In the ♂ fetus: the phallus may be enlarged
  • Non-classical CAH’
  • ← due to milder 21-hydroxylase deficiency,
  • Glucocorticoid and aldosterone production are normal, but there is overproduction of 17OHP and thus androgens.
  • Affected girls present in later childhood or adulthood with hirsutism, acne, premature/exaggerated adrenarche, menstrual irregularities, and ↓fertility, polycystic ovaries on US .
  • Asymptomatic in ♂

Diagnosis of classic CAH #25

  • Plasma 17-OH progesterone ( <5nmol/L—normal).
  • An ↑↑↑elevated level indicates 21-hydroxylase deficiency.
  • + ↓ cortizol + ↑ACTH +Plasma renin activity elevated
  • + (also see acute adrenal crisis)
  • Diagnosis of non-classic CAH
  • —17OH-P measurement
  • Interpretation of result
  • • >15nmol/L—CAH.
  • • 5–15nmol/L—proceed to ACTH stimulation test.
  • ACTH stimulation test
  • • Measure 17OHP 60min after ACTH administration.
  • • An exaggerated rise in 17OHP is seen in non-classic CAH.
  • Other investigations: Androgens
  • • In poorly controlled classic CAH (+non-classic CAH) in ♀, testosterone and androstenedione, DHEAS levels =↑
  • Molecular genetic testing !!!
  • Management of classic CAH
  • As for acute adrenal crisis : Hydrocortisone+ fludrocortisone + sodium chloride supplements are also needed, particularly in infancy
  • corrective surgery for virilisation (clitoral reduction, vaginoplasty, labial reconstruction ).
  • Management of non-classic CAH
  • -Since the major symptoms in adolescent girls include irregular menses, hirsutism and acne, the use of oral contraceptives may be sufficient to control the symptoms
  • -HC/ Prednisolone 2.5–5mg/day may be used but is often reserved to normalize ovulatory function.

CUSHING’S SYNDROME #26

CUSHING’ SYNDROME #27

  • Definition:
  • Chronic glucocorticoid excess, whatever its cause, leads to the constellation of symptoms and physical features known as Cushing syndrome.
  • It is most commonly iatrogenic, resulting from chronic glucocorticoid therapy (orally, inhalator, topically).
  • Spontaneous (endogeneous) Cushing syndrome is caused by abnormalities of the pituitary or
  • adrenal gland or
  • may occur as a consequence of ACTH or CRH secretion by nonpituitary tumors (ectopic ACTH syndrome; ectopic CRH syndrome).
  • Cushing disease is defined as the specific type of Cushing syndrome due to excessive pituitary ACTH secretion from a pituitary tumor.

Cushing’s syndrome: classification #28

  • ACTH-DEPENDENT Cushing’s syndrome
  • Pituitary adenoma (Cushing’s disease )(68-80%)
  • Nonpituitary neoplasm ( ectopic ACTH (12%), CRH syndrome (very rare))
  • Tumors causing the ectopic ACTH syndrome: small cell carcinoma of the lung (50% of cases), carcinoid tumors (lung, thymus, gut pancreas, ovary), pancreatic islet cell tumors, medullary carcinoma of the thyroid, pheocromocytoma
  • ACTH-INDEPENDENT Cushing’s syndrome
  • Iatrogenic (e.g. pharmacologic doses of prednisolone, dexamethasone)
  • Adrenal adenoma (10%) and carcinoma (8%)
  • Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia/neoplasm
  • Bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia
  • McCune Albright syndrome
  • Primary pigmented nodular adrenal disease (the Carney complex)

The effects of the glucocortcoids #29

OBESITY : #30

  • (“buffalo hump”), the rounded “moon-like” facies ( accompanied by facial plethora in most patients)
  • Skin changes
  • Atrophy of the epidermis and its underlying connective tissue leads to thinning (a transparent appearance of the skin) and facial plethora
  • Striae occur in 50%; are most commonly abdominal but may also occur over the breasts, hips, buttocks, thighs, and axillae; are typically red to purple, depressed below the skin surface secondary to loss of underlying connective tissue
  • typical moon facies, or Cushingoid facies
  • OBESITY :
  • It is classically central affecting mainly the face, neck, trunk, and abdomen, with relative sparing of the extremities
  • CUSHING’S SYNDROME –CLINICAL FEATURES

typical moon facies, or Cushingoid facies #31

  • Skin changes
  • Easy bruisability following minimal trauma (≈40%); Minor wounds and abrasions may heal slowly, and surgical incisions sometimes undergo dehiscence.
  • Acne presenting as pustular or papular lesions may ← glucocorticoid excess or hyperandrogenism.
  • Hirsutism (80% of female patients), especially facial hirsutism owing to hypersecretion of adrenal androgens.
  • Mucocutaneous fungal infections are frequent, including tinea versicolor, involvement of the nails (onychomycosis), and oral candidiasis.
  • Hyperpigmentation of the skin is rare in Cushing disease or adrenal tumors but is common in ectopic ACTH syndrome.

CARDIOVASCULAR #32

  • Effects:
  • : hypertension is a classic feature of spontaneous Cushing’s syndrome( dBP>100mmHg );
  • this, together with the established metabolic consequences of the disease ( diabetes, hyperlipidemia), is thought to explain the ↑ cardiovascular mortality in untreated cases;
  • +are at high risk of VTE (thromboembolic events), especially during active disease
  • Peripheral edema, varicose eczema, leg ulcers← immune suppression and delayed wound healing.

Slide 33 #33

  • Osteoporosis— frequently have evidence of significant osteopenia and osteoporosis.
  • multiple fragility fractures—typically of the feet, ribs, or vertebrae.
  • Back pain may be the initial complaint.
  • Compression fractures of the spine are demonstrated radiographically in 15% to 20% of patients.
  • !!! In fact, unexplained osteopenia in any young or middle-aged adult should always prompt an evaluation for Cushing syndrome, even in the absence of any other signs or symptoms of cortisol excess.
  • Muscle weakness —≈ 60% of cases; it is more often proximal and is usually most prominent in the lower extremities (myopathy).

Slide 34 #34

  • ! in childhood the commonest presentation is with poor linear growth and weight gain( !generalized obesity with central accentuation)

Slide 35 #35

  • This is very common as a result of elevated androgens (in females) and cortisol (in males and to a lesser extent in females).
  • Reproductive dysfunction
  • In women: menstrual irregularities: oligomenorrhea, amenorrhea, hypertricosis on the face; signs of masculinization (virilization): hirsutism, alopecia, acne (← usually signifies concomitant androgen excess as may occur secondary to ACTH-mediated adrenal androgen secretion/adrenal carcinoma)
  • In men: ↓libido, impotence+/- some degree of gynecomastia; some have decreased body hair and soft testes (← cortisol suppression of LH secretion →↓testosterone secretion by the testis)
  • CNS and psychologic disturbances: :anxiety, depression, poor concentration, poor memory; euphoria, including severe depression, psychosis with delusions or hallucinations, and paranoia.

Other features #36

  • Impaired Glucose Tolerance/ DM (30%)
  • Hyperlipidemia
  • Kidney stones—Calculi secondary to glucocorticoid-induced hypercalciuria occur in approximately 15% of patients
  • ↑ susceptibility to infections

Diagnosis of Cushing’s syndrome #37

  • Initial testing= confirming the presence of Cushing sdr
  • Testing for the cause of Cushing’s syndrome.

Slide 38 #38

  • For the initial testing for Cushing’s syndrome, one of the following tests based on its suitability for a given patient is recommended:
  • 1.Urinary free cortisol (UFC) (at least two measurements)
  • 2. 1-mg overnight DST (Bricaire test; 1 mg-DST)=the best screening test
  • Procedure: give dexamethasone 1 mg at 11p.m. ; check serum cortisol before(8a.m.) and at 8 a.m. (the next morning)
  • 3. Longer low-dose DST (2 mg/d for 48 h) (LDDST) (the optimal test for those with psychiatric problems, morbid obesity, alcoholism, where cortisol dynamics are often abnormal (pseudocushing).
  • Procedure: Administer 0.5mg dexamethasone 6-hourly for 48h at 9 a.m.,3 p.m., 9 p.m., and 3 a.m.; cortisol is measured at 8 a.m. at time 0 and 48h
  • (dexamethasone is not measured by most cortisol assays).
  • 4. Late-night salivary cortisol (two measurements)/alternative: the midnight serum cortisol test (cortisol samples are taken at 09:00 hours and 24:00 hours)
  • The absence of diurnal rhythm has been considered a hallmark of the diagnosis of Cushing syndrome.
  • 1.Initial testing= confirming the presence of Cushing sdr

Slide 39 #39

  • N.B. !!!!!!!!!!!! Random cortisol or morning cortisol measurements are of no value.
  • Do not use random serum cortisol or morning cortisol to test for Cushing’s syndrome because the diagnostic utility of single plasma cortisol concentrations is limited by the episodic nature of cortisol secretion and its appropriate elevations during stress. Normal plasma cortisol levels also vary with the method used and time of day the sample is obtained.
  • Diagnostic criteria that suggest Cushing’s syndrome are :
  • UFC greater than the normal range for the assay,
  • serum cortisol greater than 1.8 µg/dl (50 nmol/liter) after 1 mg dexamethasone (1-mg DST), and
  • loss of circadian rhythm -recorded using midnight or late-night salivary cortisol: (greater than the normal range for the assay)
  • or
  • a midnight serum cortisol (< than 1.8 µg/dl (50 nmol/l) effectively excludes Cushing’s syndrome; on the contrary, those with Cushing’s syndrome have high midnight cortisol levels (>100 nmol/L), though the 09:00 hours value may be normal. )
  • or
  • serum cortisol 9 a.m. >1.8 µg/dl (50 nmol/l)) after LDDST.
  • So, if the result of the test performed is suggestive for Cushing’s syndrome, another second recommended test, usually different from the initial one is employed and if the result is the same, the Cushing’s syndrome is confirmed and
  • ones should proceed to the next step- establishing the cause of Cushing’s syndrome

2. Testing for the cause of Cushing’s syndrome. #40

  • Plasma ACTH 8-9 a.m. (normal values: 9-52 pg/ml)
  • It represents the best way to distinguish between ACTH-dependent Cushung’s sdr (pituitary or nonpituitary ACTH-secreting neoplasm) and ACTH-independent hypercortisolism.
  • ACTH ↓ (<10 pg/ml) in ACTH- independent Cushing’s syndrome (primary glucocorticoid-secreting adrenal tumors) → the next step= Adrenal localizing studies: abdominal CT scan =the best (or MRI- if adrenal carcinoma is suspected).

2. Testing for the cause of Cushing’s syndrome. #41

  • ACTH ↑ (frequently >52pg/ml) or inappropriately high-normal = ACTH secreting neoplasm [Cushing disease (pituitary ACTH hypersecretion) or ectopic ACTH syndrome]
  • !!!The major challenge is identifying the source of the ACTH-secreting tumor!!!
  • MRI of the pituitary gland with gadolinium enhancement should be performed to identify the corticotroph adenoma.
  •  High-dose DXM suppression test (Liddle test -2*8) /alternative: overnight high-dose DXM suppression test
  • → distinguish pituitary causes from ectopic ACTH production.
  • ! The rational for this test is that in Cushing’s disease there is a resetting of the negative FB control of ACTH to a higher level than normal; so, in some patients with Cushing disease, the HPA axis is suppressible with supraphysiologic doses of glucocorticoids, whereas cortisol secretion is autonomous in patients with adrenal tumors and in most patients with the ectopic ACTH syndrome
  • Procedure: Give DXM 2mg/6h orally for 2 days; measure plasma cortisol at 0 and 48h/Give 8 mg of DXM as a single dose at 11 p.m. and measure plasma cortisol at 0 and the next morning

CUSHING’S SDR TREATMENT #44

  • DEPENDS ON THE CAUSE
  • Iatrogenic: remove source if possible
  • Treatment goals for Cushing’s syndrome
  • normalizing cortisol levels or action at its receptors to eliminate the signs and symptoms of CS and
  • treating comorbidities associated with hypercortisolism.
  • CUSHING’S DISEASE
  • Selective removal of a pituitary adenoma( transsphenoidal approach)= the optimal treatment (and usually the first line treatment option) in most patients
  • Pituitary radiotherapy (as second or third line treatment in patients who have failed TSS (incomplete removal) or have recurrent disease.
  • As control of cortisol levels after radiation may take months to years, medical treatment to control cortisol levels, while waiting for cortisol levels to fall, is essential)
  • Medical treatment: pharmacological inhibition of steroidogenesis/ drugs that reduce ACTH/CRH synthesis/release
  • Bilateral adrenalectomy – may be indicated for patients with very severe ACTH-dependent disease who cannot be promptly controlled by transsphenoidal surgery, radiotherapy and medical therapy (life-long replacement treatment with glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids is needed thereafter).
  • After bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing’s disease the primary corticotroph adenoma remains in situ. Therefore there is a significant risk of developing macroscopic (>1 cm) enlargement of the tumor and hyperpigmentation— the so-called Nelson’s syndrome. The administration of prophylactic radiotherapy ↓the likelihood of this complication.

Medical treatment #45

  • = the second line therapeutic option in patients who have failed surgery, who have persistent disease after surgery and in whom radiotherapy has or not employed. +during the preoperative preparation of patients or while awaiting radiotherapy to be effective or if surgery or radiotherapy is contraindicated.
  • The goal is clinical normalization using plasma cortisol levels/urinary free cortisol as a proxy endpoint , see below).
  • Pituitary-directed medical treatments- include cabergoline and pasireotide.
  • They act directly on corticotroph tumors to inhibit ACTH production.
  • Pasireotidum (Signifor ®) is a somatostatin analog that binds with high affinity to SST1, SST2, SST3, and especially SST5 subtypes of the SST receptor which is present on corticotroph tumors → at doses of 0.6-0.9 mg subcutaneously twice daily improves urinary cortisol to normal in about 30%, but carbohydrate tolerance may worsen.
  • Cabergoline, a dopaminergic agonist with high affinity for type 2 dopamine receptors, expressed on the majority of corticotroph adenomas has been shown to be effective at normalizing UFC levels in 10-30% of patients in doses of 1-7 mg/week.
  • Inhibitors of steroidogenesis- are useful in Cushing’s disease as adjuvant therapy.
  • Ketoconazole impairs adrenal and gonadal steroidogenesis by inhibiting several enzymes (400–1600 mg/d every 6–8 h),
  • Metyrapone, which inhibits p450c11, 1-6g/day;
  • Alternatives: etomidate, aminoglutethimide

Aldosterone- #48

  • is secreted from the zona glomerulosa under the primary control of angiotensin II, potassium, and corticotropin (ACTH).

Primary hyperaldosteronism and mineralocorticoid excess #49

  • Definition: the majority of cases of mineralocorticoid excess are due to excess aldosterone production, which may be primary or secondary, and are typically associated with hypertension and hypokalaemia.
  • Primary hyperaldosteronism
  • • is a disorder of autonomous aldosterone hypersecretion with suppressed (↓) renin levels.
  • • Secondary hyperaldosteronism occurs when aldosterone hypersecretion occurs secondary to ↑ circulating renin levels. This is typical of:
  • heart failure,
  • cirrhosis, or
  • nephrotic syndrome but can also be due to
  • renal artery stenosis and, occasionally,
  • a very rare renin-producing tumour (reninoma).

Primary hyperaldosteronism #50

  • Primary hyperaldosteronism is present in around 10% of hypertensive patients, representing the most prevalent form of secondary hypertension.
  • • Conn’s syndrome (aldosterone-producing adrenal adenoma (APA)) 35%.
  • • Bilateral idiopathic hyperaldosteronism (IHA) (macro- or micronodular adrenal hyperplasia) 60%.
  • • Aldosterone-producing adrenal carcinoma <1%.

Screening for primary aldosteronsim-Indications: #51

  • • Patients resistant to conventional antihypertensive medication (i.e. not controlled on three agents).
  • • Patients with hypertension stage 2 or 3 (BP> 160-179/100-109 mmHg)
  • • Hypertension associated with hypokalaemia (potassium <3.7mmol/L, irrespective of thiazide use).
  • • Hypertension developing before age of 40 years.
  • • Adrenal incidentaloma.
  • • Whenever considering secondary hypertension.
  • Other clinical features due to hipoK+ : polyuria, marked hypokalaemia →occasionally- tetany, myopathy (muscle weakness and cramping), hypokalemic periodic paralysis+ mild metabolic alkalosis
  • high risk than other patients with hypertension for target organ damage of the heart and kidney; they have a greater left ventricular mass (left ventricular hypertrophy), a significantly higher rate of cardiovascular events (eg, stroke, atrial fibrillation and myocardial infarction) than matched patients with EH who have similar degrees of hypertension duration and control

Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma #58

  • Pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (referred to together as PPGL) are very rare tumours of the sympathetic nervous system (less than 1 in 1000 cases of hypertension) that secrete catecholamines, noradrenaline (norepinephrine), adrenaline (epinephrine) and their metabolites.

90% arise in the adrenal medulla (pheochromocytomas) #59

  • 10% occur elsewhere in the sympathetic chain (paragangliomas).
  • Some are associated with MEN 2, von Hippel– Lindau’s (VHL) syndrome and neurofibromatosis.
  • Paragangliomas:
  • typically occur in the head and neck but are also found in the thorax, pelvis and bladder.
  • they may be functional or may show no/little endocrine activity ( ↓/no catecholamines secretion)
  • mutations in the succinate dehydrogenase (SDHD) gene have been shown to be strongly associated with the development of paraganglioma
  • The association of paraganglioma, bilateral adrenal phaeochromocytomas, positive family history or young age at presentation is seen in multiple endocrine neoplasms → inherited syndrome
  • Most tumours release both noradrenaline and adrenaline, but large tumours and extra-adrenal tumours produce almost entirely noradrenaline. NB !!! Epinephrine is not produced in paraganglia

Screening for P/PGL-indications: #60

  • • Patients harboring germline mutations associated with P/PGL or patients with a family history of MEN type 2 ( A or B), VHL type 2, neurofibromatosis, SDHD, SDHB mutations etc
  • • Young patients with hypertension, patients with severe hypertension, resistant to treatment - paroxysmal or sustained.
  • • Patient developing hypertensive crisis during general anaesthesia/surgery.
  • • Suspicious symptoms: headaches, diaphoresis, palpitations or tachycardia, episodic anxiety, tremor (40%), abdominal or chest pain in a hypertensive patient
  • • Patients with an adrenal incidentaloma.

Clinical features: #61

  • sustained or episodic hypertension often resistant to conventional therapy; orthostasis; hypotension,shock;
  • normotension
  • palpitation, headaches, or sweating,
  • pallor or flushing, livedo reticularis/
  • feeling of apprehension/ paresthesia, visual disturbance, seizures, chest pain, dyspnoea, weight loss, hyperglicemia or diabetes mellitus/
  • Manifestations of the associated genetic conditions: Von Recklinghausen (Type 1) Neurofibromatosis (NF-1 Gene), vonHippel-Lindau type 2, MEN2A, MEN2B
  • WHY IS IMPORTANT THE DIAGNOSIS?
  • the development of potentially fatal hypertensive crises + other
  • Complications
  • • Cardiovascular—left ventricular failure, dilated cardiomyopathy (reversible),dysrhythmias
  • • Respiratory—pulmonary oedema.
  • • Metabolic—carbohydrate intolerance, hypercalcaemia.
  • • Neurological—cerebrovascular, hypertensive encephalopathy.
  • the reversibility of all its manifestations after surgical removal of the tumour,
  • the lack of long-term efficacy of medical treatment,
  • the appreciable incidence of malignancy (approximately 15-20%)
  • the implications of the identification of an underlying genetic cause.

Management of Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma #66

  • Surgical resection is curative in the majority of patients.
  • Surgery may be laparoscopic if the tumour is small and apparently benign while open resection is recommended for large (eg, >6 cm) or invasive pheochromocytomas to ensure complete tumor resection, prevent tumor rupture, and avoid local recurrence.
  • Open resection is indicated also for most paragangliomas, but laparoscopic resection can be performed for small, noninvasive paragangliomas in surgically favorable locations.

Perioperative medical management #67

  • All patients with a hormonally functional PPGL should undergo preoperative blockade which should be started at least 7-14 days preoperatively to prevent perioperative cardiovascular complications
  • → an average blood pressure of ≤130/85 mm Hg, without symptomatic orthostasis.
  • They should also be well hydrated.
  • α-adrenergic receptor blockers represent the first choice class of drugs
  • eg, phenoxybenzamine (nonselective) 10 mg twice daily or
  • Doxazosin (α1 selective adrenergic receptor blocker) 2-16 mg/day, orally
  • Calcium channel blockers are excellent antihypertensive agents for patients with pheochromocytomas
  • eg.Nicardipine 20-40 mg/8 h,
  • Nifedipine 30-90 mg/day,
  • Amlodipine 10-20 mg/day, orally);
  • useful especially for those who develop severe orthostatic hypotension with α-adrenergic receptor blockers.
  • are the most often used add-on drug class to further improve blood pressure control in patients already treated with α-adrenergic receptor blockers.
  • Preoperative coadministration of β-adrenergic receptor blockers (eg. propranolol, atenolol) is indicated to control tachycardia only after 3-4 days of α-adrenergic receptor blockers administration.
  • → Use of β-adrenergic receptor blockers in the absence of an α-adrenoceptor blocker is not recommended because of the potential for hypertensive crisis due to unopposed stimulation of α-adrenergic receptors.
